description: Valtuutus is a high-performance Relationship-Based Access Control (ReBAC) authorization library for .NET inspired by Google Zanzibar, for fine-grained permissions in ASP.NET Core and .NET applications.
releaseNotes:
## Summary

Valtuutus 3.0.1 restores reading your own writes without a snap token, which 3.0.0 broke. No migration; upgrade from 3.0.0 by bumping the packages.

## Fixes

- **A request without a snap token sees every write that returned before it (#390). Regression in 3.0.0.**
  - In 3.0.0, a request without a token read at the latest settled token, with or without caching. While a write that took an older id was still open, a write that had already committed and returned stayed invisible to such requests: a check right after a write could still answer with the old state. 2.x saw the write.
  - Now a write or delete returns once every request without a token can see it, on any node, with or without caching. To get there, a committed write waits for the writes that took an older id and are still open to end. Reads are unchanged.
  - A write in your own transaction (an  overload that takes a transaction) waits in . Call it after committing if requests without a token must see the write.
  - With caching, the cache's latest token reaches the write before it returns, so requests without a token on the node that wrote see it. A write that rolled back no longer leaves those requests behind until  expires.
  - **New option ** (default 5 seconds) bounds the wait. A transaction you own and keep open makes concurrent writes wait for it, up to this long; past it the write returns anyway, and requests without a token see it once the older write ends.  turns the wait off (3.0.0 behaviour).
  - **Cost:** writes that don't overlap pay about one extra round trip (Postgres p50 1.38 → 1.50 ms). Overlapping writes wait for older ones: with 16 concurrent writers, throughput drops 11% (Postgres), 14% (SQL Server), 17% (MySQL).
  - See [Reading your own writes](Storing Data.md#reading-your-own-writes).
- **The settle wait runs on the real clock (#391).** With a  registered that stands still (such as  in tests), a write that had to wait more than one round hung. The wait now uses the system clock; the registered one still dates writes.
